knowledgeBase.summary: Practical bash scripting reference covering syntax, variables, control flow, functions, string manipulation, file operations, process control, networking commands, and battle-tested one-liners for daily automation and troubleshooting.

sections.title: Bash Basics
sections.content:
Every bash script should start with a shebang line: #!/bin/bash

Making a script executable and running it:
chmod +x script.sh
./script.sh
bash script.sh          # alternative, doesn't require execute bit

Comments use #:
# this is a comment

Exit codes — 0 means success, non-zero means failure:
exit 0                  # success
exit 1                  # generic failure
echo $?                  # check the exit code of the last command

Running multiple commands:
cmd1; cmd2               # run sequentially regardless of result
cmd1 && cmd2              # run cmd2 only if cmd1 succeeds
cmd1 || cmd2               # run cmd2 only if cmd1 fails

Quoting rules: double quotes allow variable expansion ("$VAR"), single quotes are literal ('$VAR' prints literally), backticks or $() capture command output: result=$(ls -la).

Strict mode for safer scripts (catches errors early):
set -euo pipefail
# -e: exit on any error
# -u: error on undefined variables
# -o pipefail: catch errors in piped commands, not just the last one

sections.title: Variables & Arrays
sections.content:
No spaces around = when assigning:
NAME="value"
NUM=42

Using variables:
echo "$NAME"
echo "${NAME}_suffix"     # braces needed when concatenating

Default values:
echo "${VAR:-default}"    # use 'default' if VAR is unset or empty
echo "${VAR:=default}"    # same, but also assigns default to VAR

Arrays:
ARR=("apple" "banana" "cherry")
echo "${ARR[0]}"           # first element
echo "${ARR[@]}"           # all elements
echo "${#ARR[@]}"          # array length
ARR+=("date")               # append an element

Looping over an array:
for item in "${ARR[@]}"; do
  echo "$item"
done

Associative arrays (bash 4+):
declare -A MAP
MAP[key1]="value1"
MAP[key2]="value2"
echo "${MAP[key1]}"
for key in "${!MAP[@]}"; do
  echo "$key => ${MAP[$key]}"
done

Environment vs local variables: export VAR=value makes it available to child processes; without export it's local to the current shell.

sections.title: Control Flow
sections.content:
If statements:
if [ "$VAR" = "value" ]; then
  echo "match"
elif [ "$VAR" = "other" ]; then
  echo "other match"
else
  echo "no match"
fi

Common test conditions:
[ -f file.txt ]      # file exists
[ -d /path ]          # directory exists
[ -z "$VAR" ]          # string is empty
[ -n "$VAR" ]          # string is not empty
[ "$A" -eq "$B" ]       # numeric equal
[ "$A" -gt "$B" ]       # numeric greater than
[ "$A" = "$B" ]          # string equal

For loops:
for i in 1 2 3; do echo $i; done
for i in $(seq 1 10); do echo $i; done
for file in *.txt; do echo "$file"; done

While loops:
while [ $i -lt 10 ]; do
  echo $i
  i=$((i+1))
done

Reading lines from a file safely:
while IFS= read -r line; do
  echo "$line"
done < file.txt

Case statements:
case "$VAR" in
  start) echo "starting" ;;
  stop) echo "stopping" ;;
  *) echo "unknown" ;;
esac

Break and continue work inside loops as expected: break exits the loop, continue skips to the next iteration.

sections.title: Functions
String Manipulation
sections.content:
Length:
echo "${#VAR}"

Substring extraction:
echo "${VAR:0:5}"          # first 5 characters
echo "${VAR: -5}"          # last 5 characters (space before - matters)

Replace:
echo "${VAR/old/new}"      # replace first occurrence
echo "${VAR//old/new}"     # replace all occurrences

Remove prefix/suffix:
echo "${VAR#prefix}"        # remove shortest matching prefix
echo "${VAR##prefix}"       # remove longest matching prefix
echo "${VAR%suffix}"        # remove shortest matching suffix
echo "${VAR%%suffix}"       # remove longest matching suffix

Uppercase/lowercase (bash 4+):
echo "${VAR^^}"             # uppercase
echo "${VAR,,}"             # lowercase

Splitting a string into an array:
IFS=',' read -ra PARTS <<< "a,b,c"
echo "${PARTS[1]}"           # b

String contains check:
if [[ "$VAR" == *"substring"* ]]; then echo "contains it"; fi

Trimming whitespace:
VAR=$(echo "$VAR" | xargs)    # quick trim using xargs side-effect

Using sed for replacements in text:
echo "$VAR" | sed 's/old/new/g'

sections.title: File Operations
sections.content:
Reading a file line by line (safe method, preserves whitespace):
while IFS= read -r line; do
  echo "$line"
done < input.txt

Writing to a file:
echo "text" > file.txt        # overwrite
echo "text" >> file.txt        # append
cat <<EOF > file.txt            # heredoc, multi-line write
line 1
line 2
EOF

Checking file existence and type:
[ -e path ]    # exists (file or directory)
[ -f path ]    # is a regular file
[ -d path ]    # is a directory
[ -r path ]    # is readable
[ -w path ]    # is writable
[ -x path ]    # is executable

File age and size checks:
[ -f file.txt ] && [ $(find file.txt -mmin +60) ]    # modified more than 60 min ago
stat -c%s file.txt                                     # file size in bytes

Temp files safely:
TMPFILE=$(mktemp)
trap 'rm -f "$TMPFILE"' EXIT      # ensures cleanup even if script errors out

Backup before overwriting:
cp file.txt file.txt.bak.$(date +%Y%m%d)

sections.title: Process Control
sections.content:
Running in background and waiting:
long_task &
PID=$!
wait $PID
echo "task finished"

Running multiple background tasks and waiting for all:
task1 & task2 & task3 &
wait
echo "all tasks finished"

Trapping signals for cleanup (very useful in scripts that create temp resources):
trap 'echo "cleaning up"; rm -f /tmp/lockfile' EXIT INT TERM

Simple lockfile pattern to prevent concurrent script runs:
LOCKFILE=/tmp/myscript.lock
if [ -f "$LOCKFILE" ]; then
  echo "already running"
  exit 1
fi
touch "$LOCKFILE"
trap 'rm -f "$LOCKFILE"' EXIT

Timeout on a command:
timeout 10s long_running_command

Checking if a command exists before using it:
if ! command -v jq &> /dev/null; then
  echo "jq is not installed"
  exit 1
fi

Subshells vs current shell: (command) runs in a subshell (variables don't leak back), { command; } runs in the current shell.

sections.title: Networking Commands
sections.content:
Quick connectivity check in a script:
if ping -c 1 -W 2 8.8.8.8 &> /dev/null; then
  echo "network is up"
else
  echo "network is down"
fi

Waiting for a service to become available (common in deploy scripts):
until curl -sf http://localhost:8080/health > /dev/null; do
  echo "waiting for service..."
  sleep 2
done

Downloading and checking exit code:
if curl -fsSL -o file.tar.gz https://example.com/file.tar.gz; then
  echo "download succeeded"
else
  echo "download failed" >&2
  exit 1
fi

Extracting JSON fields from an API response using jq:
RESPONSE=$(curl -s https://api.example.com/data)
VALUE=$(echo "$RESPONSE" | jq -r '.field.subfield')

Simple port check inside a script:
if nc -z -w 2 host 5432; then
  echo "port open"
fi

Getting your own external IP:
curl -s ifconfig.me
curl -s ipinfo.io/ip

sections.title: Script Best Practices
sections.content:
Always start scripts with strict mode:
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail
IFS=$'\n\t'

Quote your variables — unquoted variables break on spaces and glob-expand unexpectedly:
# Bad:  rm $FILE
# Good: rm "$FILE"

Use [[ ]] instead of [ ] for conditionals in bash specifically (more features, fewer footguns with empty variables):
if [[ -z "$VAR" ]]; then ...

Always validate input arguments at the top of a script:
if [ $# -eq 0 ]; then
  echo "Usage: $0 <arg>" >&2
  exit 1
fi

Use readonly for constants:
readonly MAX_RETRIES=3

Log with timestamps for easier debugging later:
log() { echo "[$(date '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S')] $*"; }
log "starting process"

Prefer $() over backticks for command substitution — nests more cleanly.

Check scripts with shellcheck before deploying — catches a huge class of quoting and logic bugs:
shellcheck script.sh

Make scripts idempotent where possible — running twice should be safe (check before creating, use mkdir -p, etc).

sections.title: Common One-Liners
sections.content:
Find and kill a process on a port:
lsof -ti:8080 | xargs kill -9

Count lines in a file:
wc -l file.txt

Find the 10 largest files in a directory tree:
find . -type f -exec du -h {} + | sort -rh | head -10

Replace text in all files in a directory:
find . -name "*.txt" -exec sed -i 's/old/new/g' {} +

Monitor a log file and trigger on a pattern:
tail -f app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

Get the size of all subdirectories sorted:
du -h --max-depth=1 | sort -rh

Count occurrences of each unique line:
sort file.txt | uniq -c | sort -rn

Backup a directory with timestamp:
tar -czf backup-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S).tar.gz /path/to/dir

Find files modified in the last hour:
find . -mmin -60 -type f

Generate a random password:
openssl rand -base64 16

Check disk usage and alert if over threshold (useful in cron):
USAGE=$(df / | tail -1 | awk '{print $5}' | tr -d '%')
[ "$USAGE" -gt 90 ] && echo "Disk usage critical: ${USAGE}%"

Parallel execution of a command over a list:
cat hosts.txt | xargs -P 4 -I {} ssh {} 'uptime'

sections.title: Signal Handling and Cleanup Logic
sections.content:
Bash scripts often interact with external processes or create temporary files that require cleanup upon termination. Relying on scripts to finish naturally is insufficient for robust applications. The `trap` command allows scripts to intercept signals and execute cleanup functions, ensuring a consistent state regardless of how the script exits.

### Core Concept
The syntax for `trap` is `trap 'command' signal_list`. The `signal_list` includes standard POSIX signals. The most critical signals for script lifecycle management are:
- `EXIT`: Triggered when the shell exits (includes normal completion, `exit` commands, or failures).
- `INT` (SIGINT): Triggered by `Ctrl+C`.
- `TERM` (SIGTERM): The default signal sent by `kill` to request termination.
- `ERR`: Triggered when a command returns a non-zero exit status (requires `set -E` to inherit traps in functions).

### Implementation Pattern
To handle cleanup effectively, define a dedicated function and trap it at the start of the script. Using a function ensures that the cleanup logic remains centralized and maintainable.

```bash
#!/bin/bash

cleanup() {
  local exit_code=$?
  # Remove temporary files
  rm -f "$TEMP_FILE"
  # Kill background processes
  kill "$PID" 2>/dev/null
  echo "Cleanup complete. Exiting with status $exit_code"
  exit "$exit_code"
}

# Trap signals: EXIT, INT, TERM
trap cleanup EXIT INT TERM

# Script logic here
TEMP_FILE=$(mktemp)
```

### Best Practices
1. **Use `EXIT` for Catch-All**: Trapping `EXIT` is the most powerful method because it triggers regardless of whether the script finished successfully or was terminated by a signal. However, if you trap `EXIT`, ensure your cleanup function calls `exit` explicitly if needed, or it will continue execution based on the last command's status.
2. **Avoid Complexity in Traps**: Keep cleanup functions lightweight. If a trap function fails or hangs, it can leave the system in an inconsistent state. Avoid complex logic or long-running operations inside the trap.
3. **Signal Propagation**: When using `trap`, the signal is caught by the shell. If you need the script to actually terminate after cleanup, you must explicitly call `exit` or send the signal to the process group. Using `trap - EXIT` inside the cleanup function can prevent infinite loops if the cleanup function itself triggers an exit.
4. **Non-Maskable Signals**: Note that `SIGKILL` (signal 9) cannot be caught or ignored. If a process is sent `SIGKILL`, the trap will not execute. Always design scripts to handle `SIGTERM` gracefully, as this is the standard signal sent by orchestrators like systemd or Kubernetes when stopping services.

glossary.definition: The #! line at the top of a script that tells the OS which interpreter to use to run it.
A numeric value (0-255) a process returns on completion; 0 conventionally means success.
A child shell spawned by parentheses (command), where variable changes don't affect the parent shell.
A multi-line string literal syntax using <<EOF ... EOF, useful for writing multi-line content to a file or command.
Internal Field Separator — the character(s) bash uses to split words, commonly changed to handle CSV or tab-delimited data safely.
A bash builtin that runs a command when the script receives a specified signal (e.g. EXIT, INT, TERM), commonly used for cleanup.
Arguments passed to a script or function, accessed as $1, $2, etc, with $@ for all and $# for the count.
Capturing the output of a command into a variable, written as $(command) or the older backtick syntax.
Shell wildcard expansion, e.g. *.txt expanding to all matching filenames before the command runs.
A script or operation that produces the same result no matter how many times it's run.

commonIssues.problem: Script works when run manually but fails when run via cron
commonIssues.cause: Cron uses a minimal environment without the user's full PATH or shell profile.
commonIssues.solution: Use absolute paths for all commands and files in the script. Explicitly set PATH at the top. Source any needed profile explicitly if required: source /etc/profile.

commonIssues.problem: Variable with spaces breaks the script (word splitting)
commonIssues.cause: The variable wasn't quoted, so bash split it on whitespace and glob-expanded it.
commonIssues.solution: Always quote variable expansions: use "$VAR" instead of $VAR, especially in test conditions and command arguments.

commonIssues.problem: Script silently continues after a command fails
commonIssues.cause: Bash doesn't exit on error by default — it just moves to the next line.
commonIssues.solution: Add set -e at the top of the script to exit immediately on any non-zero exit code. Combine with set -uo pipefail for more comprehensive error catching.

commonIssues.problem: Comparing numbers with = instead of -eq gives wrong results
commonIssues.cause: = and == do string comparison; -eq, -gt, -lt etc are for numeric comparison.
commonIssues.solution: Use [ "$A" -eq "$B" ] for numbers, [ "$A" = "$B" ] for strings. Inside [[ ]], you can also use == for strings.

commonIssues.problem: Reading a file with read loses leading/trailing whitespace or backslashes
commonIssues.cause: Default read mangles whitespace and interprets backslashes unless IFS is cleared and -r is used.
commonIssues.solution: Use: while IFS= read -r line; do ... done < file.txt — this preserves the line exactly as written.

commonIssues.problem: Script hangs waiting for input unexpectedly
commonIssues.cause: A command inside the script (often a piped command) is reading from stdin and the script's stdin wasn't redirected away.
commonIssues.solution: Redirect stdin explicitly where not needed: command < /dev/null, or ensure loops reading files use < file.txt rather than accidentally reading from the terminal.

commonIssues.problem: Background process is killed when the script or terminal exits
commonIssues.cause: Child processes receive SIGHUP when the parent shell exits unless explicitly detached.
commonIssues.solution: Use nohup command & or disown after backgrounding the process to detach it from the parent shell's lifecycle.

commonIssues.problem: Array or loop behaves unexpectedly with filenames containing spaces
commonIssues.cause: Using unquoted globs or word-splitting-based iteration breaks on filenames with spaces.
commonIssues.solution: Use for file in *.txt; do (the glob itself, not a quoted string) and always quote "$file" inside the loop body.

commonIssues.problem: shellcheck flags SC2086 (double quote to prevent globbing/word splitting)
commonIssues.cause: An unquoted variable is being used where word splitting or glob expansion could cause unintended behavior.
commonIssues.solution: Wrap the variable in double quotes: "$VAR" instead of $VAR. This is one of the most common and important shellcheck warnings to fix.

commonIssues.problem: Script that worked on one server fails on another with the same OS
commonIssues.cause: Different shell is set as /bin/sh (dash vs bash) — dash doesn't support bash-specific syntax like arrays or [[ ]].
commonIssues.solution: Ensure the shebang is #!/bin/bash, not #!/bin/sh, if using any bash-specific features. Run the script explicitly with bash script.sh to bypass shebang ambiguity while debugging.
